draft.title: Urban and remote Australia
card: Wellbeing in Australia is generally high, but it is not the same everywhere. People in remote areas often have lower wellbeing than people in the major cities.
Remote areas often have lower average incomes and fewer jobs. There are also fewer services, such as hospitals, specialist doctors and schools.
Distance matters. A person in a remote town may travel hundreds of kilometres for specialist care or lessons beyond school.
On average, people in remote areas live shorter lives than people in the major cities. This is a pattern across many people, so it does not apply to every individual.
draft.remember: Remote Australia often has lower incomes, fewer services and shorter lives on average.

a.q: Which is the most likely reason people in remote Australia often have poorer health outcomes?
opts: Health services are fewer and far away
Remote towns have more hospitals than cities
Remote areas have higher average incomes
People in remote areas are never able to travel
a.why: Fewer services and long distances make it harder to get care early. Remote areas generally have fewer hospitals, not more. The option about travel uses never, but the card says only that distance makes access harder.
a.clue: Think about how far a person may need to go to see a specialist.

b.q: Tom lives on a cattle station in outback Western Australia. Which problem is he most likely to face compared with a Perth resident?
opts: A long trip to reach a hospital or specialist
More public transport choices to town
Shorter travel to a large range of shops
Easier access to many schools nearby
b.why: Remote areas often have fewer services spread over long distances, so reaching a hospital or specialist can take a long trip. The other options describe city advantages, which Tom is less likely to have.
b.clue: Which choice is about distance to services?

a.best: Health services are fewer and far away

b.best: A long trip to reach a hospital or specialist

problems.detail: The distractor 'People in remote areas are never able to travel' uses 'never', where the card says distance makes access harder. The absolute word makes it easy to rule out without knowing the idea.
The clue 'Think about how far a person may need to go to see a specialist' points straight to the only option that mentions services being far away, so it gives the answer away.
The stem asks which 'problem' Tom is likely to face, but the other three options describe advantages, not problems. The grammar of the stem alone singles out the right answer.
The clue 'Which choice is about distance to services?' leads students to the long-trip option and adds to the giveaway.
'Lessons beyond school' is unclear. It may mean further education or extra tuition, and students may not know which.

check.summary: The facts are correct and both intended answers are right. However, both questions are too easy to guess: in b the stem's word 'problem' fits only one option, in a an absolute 'never' distractor is easy to rule out, and both clues point straight to the answer. The card phrase 'lessons beyond school' is also unclear.

proposal.title: Urban and remote Australia
card: Wellbeing in Australia is generally high, but it is not the same everywhere. People in remote areas often have lower wellbeing than people in the major cities.
Remote areas often have lower average incomes and fewer jobs. There are also fewer services, such as hospitals, specialist doctors and schools.
Distance matters. A person in a remote town may travel hundreds of kilometres for specialist care or for further study, such as TAFE or university.
On average, people in remote areas live shorter lives than people in the major cities. Lower incomes and harder access to services help explain this gap, though it does not apply to every person.
proposal.remember: Remote Australia often has lower incomes, fewer services and shorter lives on average.

a.q: Which best explains why wellbeing is often lower in remote Australia?
opts: Lower incomes and fewer services, often far away
Higher incomes, but fewer people to share them with
More services, but each one costs more to use
Shorter lives, which then cause lower incomes
a.why: Remote areas often have lower incomes and fewer services, and long distances make those services harder to reach. The option about shorter lives reverses cause and effect: lower incomes and poor access help explain shorter lives, not the other way round.
a.clue: Check how the card compares remote incomes and services with cities.

b.q: Tom lives on a cattle station in outback Western Australia. Compared with a Perth resident, what is Tom more likely to experience?
opts: A long trip to see a specialist doctor
A higher average income than in Perth
A wider choice of schools close to home
A longer expected life than in Perth
b.why: Remote areas often have fewer services spread over long distances, so seeing a specialist can mean a long trip. Remote areas tend to have lower incomes, fewer schools and shorter lives on average, so the other options describe the opposite of the usual pattern.
b.clue: Recall how remote areas compare on income, services and life span.

a.best: Lower incomes and fewer services, often far away

b.best: A long trip to see a specialist doctor
